entries.sentence: The NHS suggests simple communication, steady routines and home aids, and advises carers to ask the council for a free carer's assessment.
entries.note: Summary of communication, routine, aids and carer's assessment pages.

entries.sentence: The NHS suggests speaking slowly in short sentences, keeping eye contact and giving the person time to answer.
entries.note: NHS communication advice.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a sudden change in behaviour or sudden confusion may point to a health problem such as an infection.
entries.note: Sudden change may be a health problem; infections such as UTI are common causes of sudden confusion.

entries.sentence: A carer's assessment from the council is free, and anyone over 18 can ask for one.
entries.note: Free for anyone over 18.

entries.sentence: A lasting power of attorney lets a person choose someone they trust to act for them, and sources advise making one while the person can still decide.
entries.note: LPA described; acting early stressed.

entries.sentence: In an emergency or if anyone is in immediate danger, call 999.
entries.note: 999 for immediate danger.

entries.sentence: NHS guidance suggests speaking slowly in short sentences and keeping eye contact.
entries.note: Speak slowly, short sentences, eye contact.

entries.sentence: It also suggests giving the person time to answer without rushing them.
entries.note: Give time to answer.

entries.sentence: Offering simple choices, or asking a question in a different way, can help.
entries.note: Simple choices and rephrasing.

entries.sentence: Cutting down background noise, such as a loud television or radio, and not interrupting are also suggested.
entries.note: Reduce noise, avoid interrupting.

entries.sentence: When speech becomes harder, body language and gentle touch can matter more.
entries.note: Body language and contact matter when speech is difficult.

entries.sentence: For repeated questions, the NHS says reassurance can ease things, and a visible answer such as an easy-to-read clock may help.
entries.note: Reassurance or visible answer such as a clock.

entries.sentence: It suggests listening for a theme behind the question, such as the person believing they are lost, and offering reassurance.
entries.note: Look for underlying theme e.g. believing they are lost.

entries.sentence: NHS Inform Scotland recommends a regular daily routine, which it says can encourage feelings of security, value and worth.
entries.note: Regular routine encourages security, value and worth.

entries.sentence: Daily walks are suggested for restlessness, and they can also help with sleep and bowel regularity.
entries.note: Routine including daily walks suggested for restlessness; walks help sleep and bowels.

entries.sentence: Letting the person help with simple jobs, such as laying the table or shopping, can help them feel useful.
entries.note: Simple tasks help them feel useful.

entries.sentence: For sleep, the advice includes plenty of daylight and activity during the day, no caffeine or alcohol in the evening, and limiting daytime naps.
entries.note: Daylight, activity, evening caffeine/alcohol cut, limit naps.

entries.sentence: Memory aids can be used around the home, such as pictures on cupboard doors showing what is inside.
entries.note: Labels or pictures on cupboards and doors.

entries.sentence: Other suggestions include keeping keys in one place and writing reminders to lock the door at night or turn the gas off.
entries.note: Keep keys together; reminders to lock door/turn gas off.

entries.sentence: For wandering, the NHS suggests going with the person on walks or considering telecare, such as tracking devices and alarms.
entries.note: Accompany on walks; telecare.

entries.sentence: An occupational therapist might be able to suggest changes to the home to help with daily routines.
entries.note: OT may suggest home changes.

entries.sentence: The NHS says that if a change in behaviour comes on suddenly, the cause may be a health problem.
entries.note: Sudden behaviour change may be a health problem.

entries.sentence: It advises asking a GP for an assessment to rule out or treat any underlying cause.
entries.note: GP assessment to rule out or treat cause.

entries.sentence: Alzheimer's Society lists constipation, pain and urinary tract infections as common triggers.
entries.note: Constipation, pain, UTI typical triggers.

entries.sentence: It also suggests asking the GP to review all the person's medicines, including any bought without a prescription.
entries.note: Review all medication including non-prescription.

entries.sentence: When someone is aggressive, the NHS suggests trying to stay calm and avoiding confrontation.
entries.note: Stay calm, avoid confrontation.

entries.sentence: Doctors may check for uncontrolled pain, untreated depression, infections and side effects of medicines.
entries.note: Doctors should check pain, depression, infections, medicine side effects.

entries.sentence: The NHS adds that specialists may prescribe an antipsychotic medicine if coping strategies do not work and the person has persistent aggression or extreme distress.
entries.note: Antipsychotics may be prescribed for persistent aggression/extreme distress if coping strategies fail.

entries.sentence: Sudden confusion is different from the slow changes of dementia, and the NHS says it needs medical help straight away.
entries.note: NHS: seek medical help immediately if someone suddenly becomes confused.

entries.sentence: The NHS advises calling 999 for sudden confusion rather than driving the person to A&E.
entries.note: Advises 999 rather than driving to A&E.

entries.sentence: It lists infection as a common cause, with urinary tract infections frequent in older people and people with dementia.
entries.note: Infection; UTIs frequent in older people/with dementia.

entries.sentence: Stroke or a mini-stroke (TIA) and low blood sugar in people with diabetes are other causes it names.
entries.note: Stroke/TIA, low blood sugar in diabetes.

entries.sentence: Alzheimer's Society advises that if you think a person with dementia has delirium, you call the GP or NHS 111 straight away.
entries.note: Seek medical help straight away by calling GP or NHS 111.

entries.sentence: NHS trusts say delirium can look like a sudden change from the person's usual behaviour.
entries.note: Delirium as sudden shift from normal behaviour.

entries.sentence: They add that delirium can be mistaken for dementia getting worse, and that finding and treating the cause early gives a better outcome.
entries.note: Delirium symptoms sometimes mistaken for worsening dementia; earlier identification better outcome.

entries.sentence: The NHS says a carer can ask for an assessment to see what might make life easier, and it is free for anyone over 18.
entries.note: Free, anyone over 18.

entries.sentence: It is arranged through the local council's adult social services.
entries.note: Request through council adult social services.

entries.sentence: The assessor asks how caring affects the carer's physical and mental health, work, free time and relationships.
entries.note: What assessment covers.

entries.sentence: A carer can have one even if the person they care for does not want their own needs assessed.
entries.note: Doesn't matter if person does not want needs assessed.

entries.sentence: An assessment might recommend someone to take over caring so the carer can take a break, training in how to lift safely, or help with housework and shopping.
entries.note: Possible outcomes.

entries.sentence: The NHS also advises carers to register as a carer with their GP.
entries.note: Register as carer with GP.

entries.sentence: Admiral Nurses are specialist dementia nurses who give practical and emotional support to carers, and in some areas the NHS provides them with the charity Dementia UK.
entries.note: Admiral Nurses, Dementia UK, NHS in partnership in some areas.

entries.sentence: Alzheimer's Society runs a Dementia Support Line and an online forum where carers can talk to others.
entries.note: Search summary: Alzheimer's Society Dementia Support Line and Support Forum.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes a lasting power of attorney (LPA) as a legal document that lets a person choose someone they trust to act on their behalf.
entries.note: LPA definition.

entries.sentence: There are two kinds, one for property and financial affairs and one for health and welfare.
entries.note: Two types.

entries.sentence: A person can make one or both, and can choose the same attorneys or different ones.
entries.note: Both or one; same or different attorneys.

entries.sentence: GOV.UK says LPAs are not only a way to plan for losing mental capacity through dementia.
entries.note: GOV.UK: LPAs aren't just for dementia.

entries.sentence: The forms must be signed to confirm the person has mental capacity and be witnessed, and each LPA is then registered with the Office of the Public Guardian.
entries.note: Signed with capacity, witnessed, registered with OPG.

entries.sentence: Several sources stress acting early, while the person can still make these decisions.
entries.note: Act early while capacity intact.

entries.sentence: Without an LPA, family members may have to apply to the Court of Protection to become a deputy, which can take time and be costly.
entries.note: Court of Protection deputy, time-consuming and expensive.

entries.sentence: The NHS page says a solicitor is not required, and suggests the Law Society directory and the Office of the Public Guardian for help.
entries.note: No need for solicitor; Law Society directory; OPG.

entries.sentence: Caring can be hard on the carer, and help is available at any time.
entries.note: Carer assessment covers how caring affects mental health; help available (framing).

entries.sentence: If someone is in immediate danger or at risk of serious self-harm, call 999.
entries.note: 999 for immediate danger/serious self-harm.

entries.sentence: For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which NHS pages describe as open 24 hours a day.
Anyone can call on behalf of someone else, and the call is free.
entries.note: Can call for someone else; free.

entries.sentence: Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.
entries.note: Not returned by search; Samaritans 116 123 is named in the brief.
